statement: Let $E$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space) and $T$ a [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator) on $E$ with $q = \|T\| < 1$. Then $I - T$ has a bounded inverse $R = \sum_{n \ge 0} T^n$. The series converges in operator norm, $\|R\| \le 1/(1-q)$, and $\|R - \sum_{n \le N} T^n\| \le q^{N+1}/(1-q)$ for every integer $N \ge 0$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), real or complex.
The map $T\colon E \to E$ is a linear [bounded operator](c:bounded-operator).
The [operator norm](c:operator-norm) satisfies $q = \|T\| < 1$.

conclusion: The operator $I - T$ has the bounded inverse $\sum_{n \ge 0} T^n$, with $\|R\| \le 1/(1-q)$ and the stated tail bound.

formal.difference: The declaration states that $1 - x$ is a unit in a complete normed algebra when $\|x\| < 1$. It is a related fact and does not give the tail bound.

proofs.name: Geometric series of operators
proofs.slogan: Bound the powers of $T$, sum the series in a complete space, and telescope with $I - T$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $q = 0$. In that case $T = 0$, $R = I$ and every tail is $0$. The proof uses only powers of $T$.

roles.why: Completeness of $E$ gives a limit for each Cauchy sequence $P_N x$.
Boundedness gives $\|UVx\| \le \|U\|\|V\|\|x\|$, so norms of powers are controlled.
The bound $q < 1$ makes the scalar series $\sum q^n$ converge.

steps.slogan: Bound the norm of each power $T^n$ by $q^n$.
steps.detail: For bounded operators $U$ and $V$, $\|UVx\| \le \|U\|\|V\|\|x\|$, so $\|UV\| \le \|U\|\|V\|$. Induction gives $\|T^n\| \le q^n$ for $n \ge 1$. Also $\|I\| \le 1$, including on the zero space.

steps.slogan: Show that the partial sums $P_N = \sum_{n \le N} T^n$ form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: For $m > N$, the triangle inequality gives $\|P_m - P_N\| \le \sum_{n=N+1}^m q^n \le q^{N+1}/(1-q)$. The scalar [geometric series](c:geometric-series) shows that this bound tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Define $R$ as the pointwise limit of $P_N$ and show that $R$ is bounded.
steps.detail: For each $x$, the sequence $P_N x$ is Cauchy, because $\|(P_m - P_N)x\| \le \|P_m - P_N\|\|x\|$. Completeness of $E$ gives a limit $Rx$. Limits keep sums and scalar multiples, so $R$ is linear. Also $\|Rx\| \le \|x\|/(1-q)$, so $\|R\| \le 1/(1-q)$.

steps.slogan: Let $m$ tend to infinity in the tail estimate to bound $R - P_N$.
steps.detail: For every $x$, the estimate gives $\|(R - P_N)x\| \le q^{N+1}\|x\|/(1-q)$, because the norm is continuous. So $\|R - P_N\| \le q^{N+1}/(1-q)$, and $P_N \to R$ in operator norm.

steps.slogan: Telescope the product with $I - T$ to show that $R$ is the inverse.
steps.detail: Cancellation gives $(I-T)P_N = P_N(I-T) = I - T^{N+1}$. Since $\|T^{N+1}\| \le q^{N+1} \to 0$, and multiplication by $I - T$ is continuous in operator norm, the limit gives $(I-T)R = R(I-T) = I$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness of the space turns Cauchy sequences into limits.
concepts.c:bounded-operator: Boundedness of $T$ gives the norm estimates for products and powers.
concepts.c:operator-norm: The norm $q < 1$ controls every power of $T$.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The scalar series $\sum q^n$ bounds every operator tail.

statement: For real $a, b > 0$, the [Gamma function](c:gamma-function) $\Gamma(a) = \int_0^\infty t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt$ and the [Beta integral](c:euler-beta-function) $B(a,b) = \int_0^1 s^{a-1}(1-s)^{b-1}\,ds$ are finite. Also $B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$ and $\int_0^\infty x^{a-1}(1+x)^{-a-b}\,dx = B(a,b)$.

hypotheses.text: The parameters $a$ and $b$ are real and strictly positive.
Each integral is a [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral) of a nonnegative function on an open interval.

conclusion: The integrals $\Gamma(a)$, $\Gamma(b)$ and $B(a,b)$ are finite, $B(a,b) = \Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)/\Gamma(a+b)$, and the second integral equals $B(a,b)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the product formula for complex parameters with positive real part. It is a related fact and does not state the second integral.

proofs.name: Tonelli and a substitution
proofs.slogan: Multiply two Gamma integrals, change variables to polar-like coordinates $(r, s)$, and factor.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real $a, b > 0$. All integrands are nonnegative, so Tonelli applies without extra checks.

roles.why: Positivity of $a$ and $b$ makes the integrals converge and keeps $r > 0$.
Nonnegative integrands let Tonelli factor and exchange integrals.

steps.slogan: Bound the integrands near each end to show that all the integrals are finite.
steps.detail: For $a > 0$, $t^{a-1}$ is integrable on $(0,1)$. For $t \ge 1$, $t^{a-1}e^{-t} \le Ce^{-t/2}$ for some finite $C$. So $\Gamma(a)$ is finite, and the same holds for $\Gamma(b)$ and $\Gamma(a+b)$. The Beta integrand is integrable near $0$ and near $1$, so $B(a,b)$ is finite. Also $\Gamma(a+b) > 0$, because its integrand is positive on $(1,2)$.

steps.slogan: Write the product $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)$ as one double integral over the quadrant.
steps.detail: Tonelli gives $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_{(0,\infty)^2} u^{a-1}v^{b-1}e^{-u-v}\,du\,dv$. The integrand is nonnegative, so the factorization is valid.

steps.slogan: Substitute $u = rs$ and $v = r(1-s)$ in the double integral.
steps.detail: The map $(r,s) \mapsto (rs, r(1-s))$ is a smooth bijection from $(0,\infty) \times (0,1)$ onto the quadrant, with inverse $r = u+v$, $s = u/(u+v)$. Its Jacobian is $r$. The change-of-variables formula gives the integrand $r^{a+b-1}e^{-r}s^{a-1}(1-s)^{b-1}$.

steps.slogan: Factor the transformed integral and divide by $\Gamma(a+b)$.
steps.detail: Tonelli splits the integral into $\Gamma(a+b)B(a,b)$. Division by the positive, finite $\Gamma(a+b)$ gives the ratio formula.

steps.slogan: Substitute $s = x/(1+x)$ to get the second identity.
steps.detail: Then $x = s/(1-s)$ and $dx = ds/(1-s)^2$, and $x^{a-1}(1+x)^{-a-b}\,dx = s^{a-1}(1-s)^{b-1}\,ds$. The change of variable and the finiteness of $B(a,b)$ give the integral.

steps.slogan: Collect the ratio formula and the second identity as the theorem.
steps.detail: The finiteness, the ratio formula and the second identity are the three claims of the statement.

concepts.c:gamma-function: The Gamma integrals are the objects that the product formula relates.
concepts.c:euler-beta-function: The Beta integral appears after the change of variables.
concepts.c:lebesgue-integral: Tonelli and the change of variables hold for Lebesgue integrals of nonnegative functions.

statement: Let $K$ be a field and $G$ a finite subgroup of $K^\times$. Then $G$ is a [cyclic group](c:cyclic-group). In particular, $K^\times$ is cyclic when $K$ is a [finite field](c:finite-field), and $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$ is cyclic of order $p-1$ for each prime $p$. It has $\varphi(p-1)$ generators, the primitive roots mod $p$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $K$ is a field.
The set $G$ is a finite subgroup of the multiplicative group $K^\times$.

conclusion: The group $G$ is cyclic. For a prime $p$, the group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$ is cyclic with $\varphi(p-1)$ generators.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a finite subgroup of the units of an integral domain is cyclic. It does not state the count $\varphi(p-1)$ of primitive roots.

proofs.name: Counting elements by order
proofs.slogan: Count the elements of each order with a root bound, and compare with $\sum_{d \mid m} \varphi(d) = m$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The group $G$ is not empty, because it contains $1$. The proof uses only that $X^d - 1$ has at most $d$ roots in a field.

roles.why: A field gives the root bound: $X^d - 1$ has at most $d$ roots.
Finiteness lets us sort the $m = |G|$ elements by their orders, which divide $m$.

steps.slogan: Sort the $m$ elements of $G$ by their [order](c:order-of-an-element).
steps.detail: Let $\psi(d)$ be the number of elements of $G$ of order $d$. Each order divides $m = |G|$, so $\sum_{d \mid m} \psi(d) = m$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\psi(d) \le \varphi(d)$ for each divisor $d$ of $m$.
steps.detail: If $\psi(d) = 0$, this is clear. Otherwise pick $x$ of order $d$. The $d$ powers of $x$ are distinct roots of $X^d - 1$, so they are all the roots in $K$. Each element of order $d$ is a root, so it is $x^k$, and $x^k$ has order $d/\gcd(k,d)$. Hence $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$.

steps.slogan: Prove the identity $\sum_{d \mid m} \varphi(d) = m$ by sorting fractions.
steps.detail: Sort the $m$ fractions $k/m$ for $1 \le k \le m$ by their reduced denominator $d$. The fractions with reduced denominator $d$ are $a/d$ with $\gcd(a,d) = 1$, and there are $\varphi(d)$ of them. Every divisor $d$ of $m$ occurs.

steps.slogan: Compare the two sums to get $\psi(m) = \varphi(m) \ge 1$.
steps.detail: Both sums equal $m$, and $\psi(d) \le \varphi(d)$ for every $d$. So $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$ for all $d \mid m$. In particular $\psi(m) = \varphi(m) \ge 1$. An element of order $m = |G|$ generates $G$, so $G$ is cyclic.

steps.slogan: Apply the result to $K = \mathbb{F}_p$ and count the generators.
steps.detail: Take $K = \mathbb{F}_p$ and $G = K^\times$, which has order $p - 1$. So $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$ is cyclic. By the count in the bound step, its generators are the elements of order $p-1$, and there are $\varphi(p-1)$ of them.

concepts.c:cyclic-group: The goal is to show that one element generates the whole group.
concepts.c:finite-field: The prime field case gives the cyclic unit group $(\mathbb{Z}/p)^\times$.
concepts.c:order-of-an-element: Sorting elements by order turns the problem into a count.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ the smallest prime divisor of $|G|$. If a subgroup $H$ of $G$ has [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $p$, then $H$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$. In particular, a subgroup of index $2$ is normal. This also holds for index $2$ in an infinite group.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is finite, and $p$ is the smallest prime divisor of $|G|$.
The subgroup $H$ has [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) exactly $p$ in $G$.

conclusion: The subgroup $H$ is normal in $G$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the result for a finite group and the smallest prime factor of its order. It is a related form and does not state the infinite index 2 case.

proofs.name: Action on the cosets
proofs.slogan: Let $G$ act on the $p$ cosets of $H$, bound the size of the image in $S_p$, and show that the kernel equals $H$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. For index $2$, finiteness of $G$ is not needed, because the image size $m$ divides $2! = 2$ already.

roles.why: Finiteness of $G$ makes every prime divisor of $m$ divide $|G|$, so it is at least $p$.
Index $p$ gives a set $G/H$ of $p$ points and the final comparison $[G:K] \ge p$.

steps.slogan: Let $G$ act on the $p$ left cosets of $H$ by left multiplication.
steps.detail: The set $X = G/H$ has $p$ elements, and this [group action](c:group-action) gives a homomorphism $\rho\colon G \to \operatorname{Sym}(X)$. Here $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ is the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group) $S_p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the kernel $K$ of $\rho$ is a normal subgroup inside $H$.
steps.detail: The kernel $K$ is normal in $G$. If $g \in K$, then $g$ fixes the coset $H$, so $gH = H$ and $g \in H$. Hence $K \subseteq H$.

steps.slogan: Show that the image has size $m = p^a$ for some $a \ge 0$.
steps.detail: By the first isomorphism theorem, $G/K \cong \rho(G) \le S_p$, so $m = [G:K]$ divides $p!$ by Lagrange. Also $m$ divides $|G|$, so each prime divisor of $m$ is at least $p$. Each prime divisor of $m$ divides $p!$, so it is at most $p$. Thus $p$ is the only prime divisor, and $m = p^a$.

steps.slogan: Show that $p$ divides $p!$ exactly once, so $m$ is $1$ or $p$.
steps.detail: Among the factors $1, \dots, p$ of $p!$, only $p$ itself is a multiple of $p$, and it is not a multiple of $p^2$. Since $p^a$ divides $p!$, we get $a \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Compare indices to get $K = H$, so that $H$ is normal.
steps.detail: Since $K \subseteq H$, $m = [G:K] = [G:H][H:K] = p\,[H:K] \ge p$. With $m \in \{1, p\}$, this gives $m = p$ and $[H:K] = 1$. So $H = K$ is normal.

concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: Index $p$ gives a coset set with $p$ points and the final comparison.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: The goal is to show that $H$ equals a kernel, which is normal.
concepts.c:group-action: The action on cosets gives the homomorphism to a symmetric group.
concepts.c:symmetric-group: Its order $p!$ bounds the image and limits its prime divisors.

statement: Let $H$ be an $n \times n$ [Hadamard matrix](c:hadamard-matrix): a [matrix](c:matrix) with all entries equal to $1$ or $-1$ and $HH^T = nI$. If $n > 2$, then $n$ is divisible by $4$.

hypotheses.text: The [matrix](c:matrix) $H$ has all entries in $\{1, -1\}$.
The matrix satisfies $HH^T = nI$, so two different rows are orthogonal.
The order satisfies $n > 2$, so $H$ has at least three rows.

conclusion: The order $n$ is divisible by $4$.

formal.difference: The declaration states a divisibility by 4 for a Hadamard matrix. It is a mathlib neighbour with its own form of the hypotheses.

proofs.name: Three rows and four column classes
proofs.slogan: Normalize the first row to all ones, then count the columns by the signs of two other rows.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n > 2$. The orders $1$ and $2$ are excluded, because $(1)$ and $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ are Hadamard matrices.

roles.why: Entries $\pm 1$ make each column sign flip harmless and make row sums count signs.
Orthogonality of rows gives the zero sums and the third equation.
Three distinct rows exist only when $n \ge 3$.

steps.slogan: Multiply columns by $-1$ so that the first row has only entries $1$.
steps.detail: Multiply column $j$ by $-1$ when the first row has entry $-1$ in column $j$. Each column enters a product of two rows with a square factor, so no row product changes.

steps.slogan: Show that every other row has sum $0$.
steps.detail: Every other row is orthogonal to the first row, which is all ones. So its entries add up to $0$, and it has as many entries $1$ as entries $-1$.

steps.slogan: Sort the columns into four classes by the signs in two other rows.
steps.detail: Choose rows $r_2$ and $r_3$ besides the first row. Let $a, b, c, d$ be the numbers of columns with sign pairs $(+,+)$, $(+,-)$, $(-,+)$, $(-,-)$, so $a+b+c+d = n$. Zero sums give $a+b = c+d$ and $a+c = b+d$. Orthogonality of $r_2$ and $r_3$ gives $a+d = b+c$.

steps.slogan: Solve the three equations to get $a = b = c = d$ and $n = 4a$.
steps.detail: Subtracting the second equation from the first gives $b = c$. Then the second gives $a = d$, and the third gives $2a = 2b$. So all four class sizes are equal, and $n = 4a$.

concepts.c:hadamard-matrix: The theorem is about the order of this kind of matrix.
concepts.c:matrix: Row and column operations on the entries drive the argument.

statement: Let $G$ be a simple [graph](c:graph) with $n$ vertices and $e$ edges and no cycle of length $4$. Then $e \le \frac{n}{4}(1 + \sqrt{4n-3})$. For a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph) between $X$ and $Y$ with no $4$-cycle and $m = |X|$, $\sum_{y \in Y} \binom{d(y)}{2} \le \binom{m}{2}$.

hypotheses.text: The [graph](c:graph) $G$ has no loops and no multiple edges.
Two different vertices have at most one common neighbor, because $G$ has no $4$-cycle.

conclusion: The edge count satisfies $e \le \frac{n}{4}(1 + \sqrt{4n-3})$, and the bipartite sum satisfies $\sum_{y} \binom{d(y)}{2} \le \binom{m}{2}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the double counting identity for a bipartite relation. It does not state the C4-free bound itself.

proofs.name: Counting cherries
proofs.slogan: Count the pairs of neighbors of a vertex in two ways, then bound the sum of binomials by convexity.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The bipartite sum bound is the count in step two, applied to the pairs in $X$. The edge bound uses the count for all vertices.

roles.why: Simplicity makes the degree sum $2e$ and gives a definite number of pairs.
The common-neighbor bound limits each pair to at most one cherry.

steps.slogan: Show that a graph has no $4$-cycle if and only if each pair has at most one common neighbor.
steps.detail: If distinct vertices $a$ and $b$ had two common neighbors $u$ and $v$, then $a, u, b, v$ would form a $4$-cycle. The converse is the same argument read backwards.

steps.slogan: Count the cherries $(v; \{a, b\})$ in two ways.
steps.detail: A cherry is a vertex $v$ with a pair $\{a, b\}$ of its neighbors. Counting by $v$ gives $\sum_v \binom{d(v)}{2}$, with $d(v)$ the [degree](c:vertex-degree) of $v$. Counting by the pair $\{a, b\}$ gives at most one cherry per pair, so at most $\binom{n}{2}$. In the bipartite graph, the same count with $y \in Y$ and $\{x, x'\} \subseteq X$ gives $\sum_y \binom{d(y)}{2} \le \binom{m}{2}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum of binomials from below by Jensen's inequality.
steps.detail: The function $\phi(d) = d(d-1)/2$ is convex. With mean degree $\bar d = 2e/n$ from the degree sum, Jensen's inequality gives $\sum_v \phi(d(v)) \ge n\,\bar d(\bar d - 1)/2$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two bounds and solve the quadratic inequality for $\bar d$.
steps.detail: The bounds give $n\bar d(\bar d-1)/2 \le n(n-1)/2$, so $\bar d^2 - \bar d - (n-1) \le 0$. The roots of the quadratic are $(1 \pm \sqrt{4n-3})/2$, so $\bar d \le (1 + \sqrt{4n-3})/2$. Since $e = n\bar d/2$, we get $e \le \frac{n}{4}(1 + \sqrt{4n-3})$.

concepts.c:graph: The theorem bounds the edges of a graph with no short cycle.
concepts.c:bipartite-graph: The bipartite version counts pairs on one side with neighbors on the other.

statement: Let $f\colon \{1, 2, \dots\} \to [0, \infty)$ be [non-increasing](c:monotone-sequence). Then the [series](c:series) $\sum_{n \ge 1} f(n)$ converges if and only if $\sum_{k \ge 0} 2^k f(2^k)$ converges. More exactly, $S_{2^{K+1}-1} \le T_K \le 2S_{2^K}$, where $S_N = \sum_{n \le N} f(n)$ and $T_K = \sum_{k=0}^K 2^k f(2^k)$.

hypotheses.text: The values satisfy $f(n) \ge 0$ for all $n$.
The function $f$ is [non-increasing](c:monotone-sequence): $f(n+1) \le f(n)$.

conclusion: The inequalities $S_{2^{K+1}-1} \le T_K \le 2S_{2^K}$ hold, and the two series converge together.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same equivalence for summability of a non-increasing nonnegative real sequence. It does not state the partial sum inequalities.

proofs.name: Dyadic blocks
proofs.slogan: Bound each block of terms between $2^k$ and $2^{k+1}$ above and below by multiples of $2^k f(2^k)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A finite change of $f$ at the start does not change convergence, so the test also holds when $f$ is non-increasing from some index on.

roles.why: Nonnegative terms make the partial sums non-decreasing, so bounded sums converge.
Monotonicity bounds each term of a block by the first or the last term of the block.

steps.slogan: Bound each dyadic block from above and sum the blocks to get $S_{2^{K+1}-1} \le T_K$.
steps.detail: For $2^k \le n < 2^{k+1}$, monotonicity gives $f(n) \le f(2^k)$. The block has $2^k$ terms, so its sum is at most $2^k f(2^k)$. The blocks for $k = 0, \dots, K$ partition $\{1, \dots, 2^{K+1}-1\}$.

steps.slogan: Bound each dyadic block from below to get $T_K \le 2S_{2^K}$.
steps.detail: For $2^{k-1} < n \le 2^k$ and $k \ge 1$, monotonicity gives $f(n) \ge f(2^k)$. This block has $2^{k-1}$ terms, so its sum is at least $\frac12 2^k f(2^k)$. Summing over $k = 1, \dots, K$ and adding $f(1) \ge \frac12 f(1)$ gives $S_{2^K} \ge \frac12 T_K$.

steps.slogan: Show that convergence of $\sum f(n)$ gives convergence of the condensed series.
steps.detail: If $\sum f(n) = S$, then $T_K \le 2S_{2^K} \le 2S$ for all $K$. The partial sums $T_K$ are non-decreasing and bounded, so they converge.

steps.slogan: Show that convergence of the condensed series gives convergence of $\sum f(n)$.
steps.detail: If the condensed series has sum $T$, then $S_N \le S_{2^{K+1}-1} \le T_K \le T$ for $N < 2^{K+1}$. The partial sums $S_N$ are non-decreasing and bounded, so they converge.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: The block inequalities and the two directions give the stated inequalities and the equivalence of the two series.

concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Monotone values let each block be compared with one of its end terms.
concepts.c:series: Both series are sums of nonnegative terms, so bounded partial sums imply convergence.

statement: For every complex $z$, $\sin(\pi z) = \pi z \prod_{n \ge 1}(1 - z^2/n^2)$. The [infinite product](c:infinite-product) converges absolutely, and uniformly on compact sets, to an entire [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). Its zeros are exactly the integers.

hypotheses.text: The variable $z$ is a complex number, and the $n$-th factor is $1 - z^2/n^2$.

conclusion: The product converges to an entire function with zero set $\mathbb{Z}$, and it equals $\sin(\pi z)$ for all complex $z$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the limit of the partial products for complex $z$. It is a related form and does not state the zero set.

proofs.name: Log derivative on (0,1) and the identity theorem
proofs.slogan: Prove the formula on $(0,1)$ by integrating the partial fraction expansion, then extend by the identity theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The proof uses the partial fraction expansion of $\pi \cot \pi x$ as a cited result.

roles.why: The product is entire, and the identity theorem extends the formula from $(0,1)$ to all of $\mathbb{C}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the product converges locally uniformly to an entire function with zero set $\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: On $|z| \le R$, $\sum |z^2/n^2| \le R^2 \sum 1/n^2 < \infty$. So the [infinite product](c:infinite-product) converges absolutely and uniformly on compact sets. The limit $P(z) = \pi z \prod (1 - z^2/n^2)$ is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on all of $\mathbb{C}$. Its zeros are the zeros of the factors, which are the integers.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the logarithm of the partial products on $(0,1)$.
steps.detail: For real $x$ with $0 < x < 1$, all factors are positive. Put $L_N(x) = \sum_{n \le N} \ln(1 - x^2/n^2)$, so $L_N(0) = 0$. Then $L_N'(x) = \sum_{n \le N} 2x/(x^2 - n^2)$.

steps.slogan: Show that $L_N'$ converges uniformly on $[0, r]$ to $\pi \cot \pi x - 1/x$.
steps.detail: The partial fraction expansion gives $\pi \cot \pi x - 1/x = \sum_{n \ge 1} 2x/(x^2 - n^2)$ on $(0,1)$. For $r < 1$ and $x \in [0, r]$, $|2x/(x^2-n^2)| \le 2r/((1-r^2)n^2)$. The Weierstrass M-test gives uniform convergence.

steps.slogan: Integrate the limit to show that $P(x) = \sin \pi x$ on $(0,1)$.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence lets the limit pass under the integral, so $\lim L_N(x) = \int_0^x (\pi \cot \pi t - 1/t)\,dt$. An antiderivative is $\ln(\sin \pi t / t)$, which tends to $\ln \pi$ as $t \to 0$. So the integral is $\ln(\sin \pi x/(\pi x))$, and $P_N(x)/(\pi x) \to \sin \pi x/(\pi x)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the identity from $(0,1)$ to $\mathbb{C}$ by the identity theorem.
steps.detail: Both $P$ and $z \mapsto \sin \pi z$ are entire, so they are [analytic functions](c:analytic-function). The set where their difference and all its derivatives vanish is closed, and it is open by the local identity theorem. It contains $(0,1)$, so it is all of the connected set $\mathbb{C}$.

concepts.c:infinite-product: The sine is written as a product of the factors $1 - z^2/n^2$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The limit is entire, so it is determined by its values near a real interval.
concepts.c:analytic-function: The identity theorem for analytic functions extends the equality to the whole plane.

statement: For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) satisfies $\zeta(s) = \frac{s}{s-1} - s\int_1^\infty \{t\}t^{-s-1}\,dt$, with $\{t\} = t - \lfloor t \rfloor$. The right side is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ except for a simple pole at $s = 1$. Also $\lim_{s \to 1}(\zeta(s) - \frac{1}{s-1}) = \gamma$, the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

hypotheses.text: The first formula holds for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, and the continuation is to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ with $s \ne 1$.
The symbol $\{t\}$ is the fractional part of $t$, with values in $[0, 1)$.

conclusion: The function $\zeta$ extends to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ with a simple pole at $1$, and $\zeta(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} + \gamma + O(s-1)$ at $s = 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the limit $\zeta(s) - 1/(s-1) \to \gamma$ as $s \to 1$. It does not state the integral formula or the continuation to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.

proofs.name: Abel summation
proofs.slogan: Apply Abel summation to the sum of $n^{-s}$, continue the integral to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, and read the constant from the harmonic sums.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The continuation covers $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ only. The Laurent expansion is the one at $s = 1$.

roles.why: The convergence of $N^{1-s}$ and of the integral needs $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, and the continuation uses $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
The bound $0 \le \{t\} < 1$ makes the integral converge for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply Abel summation to $n^{-s}$ with the [floor function](c:floor-function) to get the integral formula.
steps.detail: Take $a_n = 1$, so $A(t) = \lfloor t \rfloor$, and $f(t) = t^{-s}$. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, letting $N \to \infty$ gives $\zeta(s) = s\int_1^\infty \lfloor t \rfloor t^{-s-1}\,dt$. Split $\lfloor t \rfloor = t - \{t\}$ and use $s\int_1^\infty t^{-s}\,dt = s/(s-1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the integral is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
steps.detail: Let $J(s) = \int_1^\infty \{t\}t^{-s-1}\,dt$. The integrand is bounded by $t^{-\operatorname{Re} s - 1}$, which is integrable for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. Dominated convergence and Morera's theorem make $J$ holomorphic there. So the right side continues $\zeta$ and has only the pole at $s = 1$.

steps.slogan: Write $\zeta(s) - 1/(s-1) = 1 - sJ(s)$ to remove the pole.
steps.detail: Since $s/(s-1) = 1 + 1/(s-1)$, we get $\zeta(s) - 1/(s-1) = 1 - sJ(s)$. This is holomorphic at $s = 1$, with value $1 - J(1)$. So the [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) of $\zeta$ at $1$ starts with $1/(s-1)$.

steps.slogan: Identify $1 - J(1)$ with the limit of $H_N - \ln N$ by Abel summation.
steps.detail: Abel summation with $f(t) = 1/t$ gives $H_N - \ln N = 1 - \int_1^N \{t\}t^{-2}\,dt$ for the [harmonic number](c:harmonic-number) $H_N$. The right side tends to $1 - J(1)$, and the left side tends to $\gamma$ by definition. So $\lim_{s \to 1}(\zeta(s) - 1/(s-1)) = \gamma$.

concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: The function being continued, and the object of the Laurent expansion.
concepts.c:floor-function: The counting function $\lfloor t \rfloor$ is the summatory function in Abel summation.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The expansion at $s = 1$ has a simple pole and the constant term $\gamma$.
concepts.c:harmonic-number: The harmonic numbers $H_N$ define $\gamma$ and are summed by Abel summation.

statement: Let $0 \to A \to B \to C \to 0$ be a short exact sequence of [chain complexes](c:chain-complex) with chain maps $f$ and $g$. Then there is a long exact sequence $\cdots \to H_n(A) \to H_n(B) \to H_n(C) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots$ in [homology](c:homology). The map $\partial$ is the [connecting homomorphism](c:connecting-homomorphism), and it is natural.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $0 \to A_n \to B_n \to C_n \to 0$ is exact for every $n$.
The maps $f$ and $g$ commute with the differentials.

conclusion: The homology groups form a long exact sequence. The map $\partial$ sends $[z]$ to $[x]$, where $f(x) = d(y)$ and $g(y) = z$, and it is natural.

formal.difference: The declaration states exactness at one place of the homology sequence of a short exact sequence. It does not state the whole sequence or the formula for the connecting map.

proofs.name: Snake lemma in every degree
proofs.slogan: Apply the snake lemma to the quotients by boundaries and the cycles, then join the six-term sequences.
proofs.scope: The whole statement, for modules over any ring. The same proof works in any abelian category. The Bockstein map is the case $A = B$ with multiplication by $m$.

roles.why: Exact rows give the exactness of the top and bottom rows of the snake diagram.
Chain maps make the squares commute and make the vertical map well defined.

steps.slogan: Build the snake diagram for each $n$ with the map induced by $d$.
steps.detail: The top row is $A_n/dA_{n+1} \to B_n/dB_{n+1} \to C_n/dC_{n+1} \to 0$. The bottom row is $0 \to Z_{n-1}(A) \to Z_{n-1}(B) \to Z_{n-1}(C)$. The vertical map is $[y] \mapsto d(y)$. It is well defined because $d(dw) = 0$, and $d(y)$ is a cycle.

steps.slogan: Show that the top row is exact.
steps.detail: The map on $C$ is onto because $g$ is onto, and $g \circ f = 0$. Let $g(y) = d(w)$. Choose $v$ with $g(v) = w$. Then $g(y - dv) = 0$, so $y - dv = f(x)$, and $[y] = [f(x)]$.

steps.slogan: Show that the bottom row is exact.
steps.detail: The left map is injective because $f$ is. Let $y$ be a cycle of $B$ with $g(y) = 0$. Then $y = f(x)$. Also $f(dx) = d(y) = 0$, so $dx = 0$ because $f$ is injective. Hence $y$ comes from a cycle of $A$.

steps.slogan: Apply the snake lemma to get a six-term exact sequence with the formula for $\partial$.
steps.detail: The kernel of the vertical map is $H_n$ and its cokernel is $H_{n-1}$, for $A$, $B$ and $C$. The snake lemma gives the exact sequence $H_n(A) \to H_n(B) \to H_n(C) \xrightarrow{\partial} H_{n-1}(A) \to H_{n-1}(B) \to H_{n-1}(C)$. Its connecting map lifts $z$ to $y$, applies $d$, and pulls back along $f$.

steps.slogan: Join the six-term sequences for all $n$ into one long exact sequence.
steps.detail: Each term of the long sequence is an inner term of some six-term sequence. Neighboring pieces use the same maps. So exactness at every inner term gives exactness of the long sequence.

steps.slogan: Show that $\partial$ is natural for maps of short exact sequences.
steps.detail: A map of short exact sequences commutes with lifts, with $d$, and with pull-backs. So the formula for $\partial$ gives a commuting square.

concepts.c:chain-complex: The theorem is about three chain complexes and the maps between them.
concepts.c:homology: Kernels and cokernels of the vertical map are the homology groups.
concepts.c:connecting-homomorphism: The snake lemma builds $\partial$ from the lift-and-pull-back formula.

statement: Let $p\colon E \to X$ be a [covering space](c:covering-space) map. A path in $X$ has a unique lift through each point over its start. A homotopy has a unique lift for each lift of its start. Paths homotopic relative to end points have lifts with the same end point. Hence the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) of the circle is $\mathbb{Z}$, by the [winding number](c:winding-number).

hypotheses.text: The map $p$ is a covering map: each point of $X$ has an open set $U$ whose preimage is a disjoint union of sheets that $p$ maps homeomorphically onto $U$.
The paths have domain $[0,1]$, which is [compact](c:compact-space) and connected.
For the last part, the cover is $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ is contractible.

conclusion: Path lifts and homotopy lifts exist and are unique. Homotopic paths with the same end points lift to paths with the same end point. The winding number gives an isomorphism $\pi_1(S^1) \to \mathbb{Z}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states existence of path lifts for a covering map. It does not state uniqueness, homotopy lifting or the circle.

proofs.name: Lift in pieces and use connectedness
proofs.slogan: Lift a path piece by piece on sheets, extend to homotopies by a tube argument, and read the circle from the real line.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for paths and homotopies on $[0,1]$. Lifting from other spaces needs more hypotheses.

roles.why: Sheets over a small set $U$ give local inverses of $p$ for the lifts.
Compactness gives a Lebesgue number, and connectedness gives uniqueness.
Contractibility of $\mathbb{R}$ lets the straight-line homotopy kill loops of winding number zero.

steps.slogan: Show that two lifts of a path with the same start are equal.
steps.detail: The set where two lifts agree is closed, because different points over one point lie in disjoint sheets. It is open, because $p$ is injective on a sheet. It contains $0$, and $[0,1]$ is connected, so it is everything.

steps.slogan: Cut the interval into pieces that map into evenly covered sets, and lift each piece.
steps.detail: The sets $\gamma^{-1}(U_\alpha)$ cover $[0,1]$. A Lebesgue number gives a partition $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_n = 1$ with $\gamma([t_{i-1}, t_i])$ in one $U_i$. Define the lift on each piece by $(p|_S)^{-1} \circ \gamma$ on the sheet $S$ that holds the previous end point. The pasting lemma joins the pieces.

steps.slogan: Lift a homotopy by lifting each path and checking continuity near each parameter.
steps.detail: Lift each path $H(s, \cdot)$ from $f(s)$. For $s_0$, take a partition for $H(s_0, \cdot)$. The tube lemma gives a neighborhood $N$ of $s_0$ with $H(N \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]) \subseteq U_i$. By induction on $i$, shrink $N$ so that $\tilde H(s,t) = (p|_{S_i})^{-1} H(s,t)$ there. So $\tilde H$ is continuous. Uniqueness follows from the path case.

steps.slogan: Show that homotopic paths relative to end points have lifts with equal end points.
steps.detail: Lift the homotopy from the constant lift $f(s) = e$. The path $s \mapsto \tilde H(s,1)$ lies in a discrete fiber, so it is constant. By uniqueness, $\tilde H(0, \cdot)$ and $\tilde H(1, \cdot)$ are the lifts of the two paths from $e$, and their end points agree.

steps.slogan: Prove that $w(\gamma) = \Gamma(1) - \Gamma(0)$ is a group isomorphism onto $\mathbb{Z}$.
steps.detail: The number $w(\gamma)$ is an integer, and it depends only on the class of $\gamma$ by the end point step. Translating a lift by an integer gives $w(\gamma \cdot \delta) = w(\gamma) + w(\delta)$. The path $t \mapsto x_0 + nt$ gives onto. If $w(\gamma) = 0$, the lift is a loop in $\mathbb{R}$, and the straight-line homotopy projects to a homotopy to the constant loop. So $w$ is injective.

concepts.c:covering-space: Local inverses on sheets let us build lifts piece by piece.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The last step identifies this group of the circle.
concepts.c:winding-number: The integer $w(\gamma)$ is the winding number and gives the isomorphism.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the interval gives a Lebesgue number and a finite partition.

statement: Let $X \ge 0$ be a [random variable](c:random-variable) with $E[X^2] < \infty$ and [expected value](c:expected-value) $\mu > 0$. Then $P(X > 0) \ge \mu^2/E[X^2]$ and $P(X = 0) \le \operatorname{Var} X/\mu^2$. The first bound is never weaker than the second. For $X = \sum_i 1_{A_i}$, $\operatorname{Var} X = \sum_i p_i(1-p_i) + \sum_{i \ne j}(P(A_i \cap A_j) - p_i p_j)$.

hypotheses.text: The variable $X$ is nonnegative and in $L^2$, and $\mu > 0$.
For the variance formula, $X$ is a finite sum of indicators of events $A_i$ with $p_i = P(A_i)$.

conclusion: The bounds $P(X>0) \ge \mu^2/E[X^2]$ and $P(X=0) \le \operatorname{Var} X/\mu^2$ hold, the first is stronger, and the variance of an indicator sum has the stated form.

formal.difference: The declaration states the Chebyshev bound for the measure of a deviation set. It is related to the second bound only and does not state the first bound or the indicator formula.

proofs.name: Chebyshev and Cauchy-Schwarz
proofs.slogan: Get the second bound from Chebyshev's inequality and the first from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, then compare them.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The method shows that $X > 0$ occurs, but it does not construct a witness. The sign of $X$ matters only in the first bound.

roles.why: Finite second moment makes the variance finite and the Cauchy-Schwarz step valid.
A finite sum of indicators lets us expand the variance by bilinearity.

steps.slogan: Expand the [variance](c:variance) of an indicator sum by bilinearity of covariance.
steps.detail: We have $\operatorname{Var}(\sum Y_i) = \sum_i \sum_j \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j)$. For indicators, $\operatorname{Cov}(1_{A_i}, 1_{A_i}) = p_i(1-p_i)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(1_{A_i}, 1_{A_j}) = P(A_i \cap A_j) - p_i p_j$. This is the variance formula.

steps.slogan: Bound $P(X = 0)$ by Chebyshev's inequality.
steps.detail: If $X = 0$, then $|X - \mu| = \mu$. So $\{X = 0\} \subseteq \{|X - \mu| \ge \mu\}$, and Chebyshev gives $P(X=0) \le \operatorname{Var} X/\mu^2$.

steps.slogan: Bound $P(X > 0)$ by expanding a square and choosing the best multiplier.
steps.detail: Let $q = P(X>0)$. Then $q > 0$, because $\mu > 0$. For real $\lambda$, $0 \le E[(X - \lambda 1_{X>0})^2] = E[X^2] - 2\lambda\mu + \lambda^2 q$, because $X 1_{X>0} = X$. Take $\lambda = \mu/q$ to get $q \ge \mu^2/E[X^2]$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two bounds with $u = \operatorname{Var} X/\mu^2$.
steps.detail: We have $E[X^2] = \mu^2(1+u)$, so $\mu^2/E[X^2] = 1/(1+u)$. Also $1/(1+u) \ge 1 - u$, because $(1+u)(1-u) = 1 - u^2 \le 1$. So the first bound is never weaker.

steps.slogan: Collect the three claims and the use in a sequence of variables.
steps.detail: The steps above prove both bounds, the comparison and the variance formula. If $\operatorname{Var} X_n/(E X_n)^2 \to 0$, then $P(X_n = 0) \to 0$. If the ratio tends to a finite $u$, then $\liminf P(X_n > 0) \ge 1/(1+u)$.

concepts.c:random-variable: The count of objects is a nonnegative random variable.
concepts.c:expected-value: The mean $\mu$ appears in both bounds and in the multiplier.
concepts.c:variance: The variance controls the chance that $X$ is far from $\mu$.

statement: Let $A$ be a real $m \times n$ matrix, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The [linear program](c:linear-programming) (P) maximizes $c^T x$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$. Its dual (D) minimizes $b^T y$ subject to $A^T y \ge c$, $y \ge 0$. Then $c^T x \le b^T y$ for feasible pairs. If (P) is feasible and bounded, both have optimal solutions with equal values, and optimality is complementary slackness.

hypotheses.text: All data are real, and vector inequalities hold in every coordinate.
For strong duality, (P) has a feasible point and its supremum $v^*$ is finite.

conclusion: Weak duality holds. Under the hypothesis, [linear programming duality](c:linear-programming-duality) holds: (P) and (D) have optimal solutions with equal values. Feasible $x$ and $y$ are optimal if and only if they satisfy complementary slackness.

formal.difference: The declaration states a separation result for a point and a closed convex cone, which is the tool behind the Farkas lemma. It does not state linear program duality.

proofs.name: Farkas alternative on the dual system
proofs.slogan: Prove weak duality directly, then show that the dual system is solvable by ruling out a Farkas certificate.
proofs.scope: The whole statement under the two listed hypotheses. The unbounded case is covered by weak duality only.

roles.why: Real data make the sign arguments and the Farkas lemma valid.
Feasibility and a finite supremum rule out both certificate cases.

steps.slogan: Prove weak duality by chaining the primal and dual inequalities.
steps.detail: For feasible $x$ and $y$, $c^T x \le (A^T y)^T x = y^T(Ax) \le y^T b$. The first step uses $x \ge 0$ and $A^T y \ge c$. The last step uses $y \ge 0$ and $Ax \le b$.

steps.slogan: Write the wish for a dual point of value at most $v^*$ as a linear system.
steps.detail: Seek $z = (y, s, t) \ge 0$ with $A^T y - s = c$ and $b^T y + t = v^*$. A solution gives $y \ge 0$ with $A^T y \ge c$ and $b^T y \le v^*$. Write the system as $Mz = d$.

steps.slogan: Assume that the system has no solution and take the Farkas certificate.
steps.detail: The Farkas alternative separates $d$ from the [convex cone](c:convex-cone) of the columns of $M$. It gives $w = (w_1, \lambda)$ with $M^T w \ge 0$ and $d^T w < 0$. Put $\tilde x = -w_1$. Then $\tilde x \ge 0$, $A\tilde x \le \lambda b$, $\lambda \ge 0$ and $c^T \tilde x > \lambda v^*$.

steps.slogan: Show that the certificate gives a contradiction in both cases $\lambda > 0$ and $\lambda = 0$.
steps.detail: If $\lambda > 0$, then $\tilde x/\lambda$ is feasible with value above $v^*$. If $\lambda = 0$, then $x_0 + \tau\tilde x$ is feasible for all $\tau \ge 0$ with value tending to $\infty$. Both cases contradict the definition of $v^*$.

steps.slogan: Deduce a dual optimum with value $v^*$.
steps.detail: The system has a solution, so there is $y \ge 0$ with $A^T y \ge c$ and $b^T y \le v^*$. By weak duality $b^T y \ge v^*$. So $b^T y = v^*$, and $y$ is optimal.

steps.slogan: Apply the same argument to the dual to get a primal optimum.
steps.detail: Rewrite (D) as the maximization of $-b^T y$ subject to $-A^T y \le -c$, $y \ge 0$. It is feasible and bounded with supremum $-v^*$. The previous steps give a feasible $x$ with $c^T x = v^*$, so (P) has an optimum.

steps.slogan: Prove complementary slackness from the gap identity.
steps.detail: For feasible $x$ and $y$, $b^T y - c^T x = y^T(b - Ax) + x^T(A^T y - c)$, and both terms are at least $0$. The gap is $0$ exactly when every product is $0$. By strong duality, optimal pairs have gap $0$, and a pair with gap $0$ is optimal by weak duality.

concepts.c:linear-programming: The primal and dual problems are linear programs.
concepts.c:linear-programming-duality: The theorem states weak and strong duality for the pair.
concepts.c:convex-cone: The Farkas alternative separates a point from the cone of the columns of $M$.

statement: Let $q$ be a prime power and $N_q(n)$ the number of monic [irreducible polynomials](c:irreducible-polynomial) of degree $n$ over the [finite field](c:finite-field) $\mathbb{F}_q$. Then $x^{q^n} - x$ is the product of all monic irreducible polynomials whose degree divides $n$. So $\sum_{d \mid n} d\,N_q(d) = q^n$ and $N_q(n) = \frac1n \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(n/d) q^d \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The number $q$ is a prime power, and $\mathbb{F}_q$ is the field with $q$ elements.
The number $n$ is a positive integer, and $\mu$ is the Möbius function.

conclusion: The polynomial $x^{q^n} - x$ is the product of the monic irreducibles of degree dividing $n$. The count satisfies the divisor sum and the Möbius formula, and $N_q(n) \ge 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that a field of degree $d$ embeds in one of degree $n$ over a finite field exactly when $d$ divides $n$. It does not state the polynomial count.

proofs.name: Frobenius order and the divisor test
proofs.slogan: Show that an irreducible of degree $d$ divides $x^{q^n} - x$ exactly when $d$ divides $n$, then count degrees and invert.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for each $q$ and $n \ge 1$. The count is for monic polynomials.

roles.why: The field $\mathbb{F}_q$ has $q^n = 0$ in characteristic $p$, so the derivative of $x^{q^n} - x$ is $-1$.
Positive $n$ gives the divisor sum over a finite set, and Möbius inversion applies.

steps.slogan: Show that $P = x^{q^n} - x$ has no repeated factor.
steps.detail: The derivative is $q^n x^{q^n - 1} - 1 = -1$, because $q^n = 0$ in $\mathbb{F}_q$. So $\gcd(P, P') = 1$, and no irreducible factor of $P$ repeats. Hence $P$ is the product of the distinct monic irreducible polynomials that divide it.

steps.slogan: Show that a monic irreducible $f$ of degree $d$ divides $P$ if and only if $d$ divides $n$.
steps.detail: Let $K = \mathbb{F}_q[x]/(f)$, a field with $q^d$ elements, and $\alpha$ the class of $x$. The Frobenius map $\varphi(y) = y^q$ fixes $\mathbb{F}_q$ and has order exactly $d$, since $y^{q^d} = y$ and $x^{q^r} - x$ has at most $q^r$ roots. Now $f \mid P$ if and only if $\varphi^n(\alpha) = \alpha$. This holds if and only if $\varphi^n = \mathrm{id}$, because $\alpha$ generates $K$. That means $d \mid n$.

steps.slogan: Compare degrees in the factorization of $P$.
steps.detail: By the first two steps, $x^{q^n} - x = \prod_{d \mid n} \prod_{\deg f = d} f$. Comparing degrees gives $q^n = \sum_{d \mid n} d\,N_q(d)$.

steps.slogan: Invert the divisor sum by Möbius inversion.
steps.detail: Put $g(n) = q^n$ and $h(d) = d\,N_q(d)$. Then $g(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} h(d)$ for all $n$. The inversion formula gives $n\,N_q(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} \mu(n/d) q^d$.

steps.slogan: Show that $N_q(n) \ge 1$ by bounding the smaller degrees.
steps.detail: For $n = 1$, $N_q(1) = q$. For $n \ge 2$ let $m = \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$. Since $d\,N_q(d) \le q^d$, we get $n\,N_q(n) \ge q^n - \sum_{d=1}^m q^d \ge q^n - q^{m+1} + q \ge q > 0$.

steps.slogan: Collect the factorization, the formulas and the existence of extensions of every degree.
steps.detail: The steps prove the product formula, the divisor sum, the Möbius formula and $N_q(n) \ge 1$. So $\mathbb{F}_q$ has an extension of every degree $n$.

concepts.c:irreducible-polynomial: The theorem counts the irreducible factors of $x^{q^n}-x$.
concepts.c:finite-field: The fields $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $\mathbb{F}_q[x]/(f)$ carry the Frobenius map.

statement: Let $f$ be [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) in $x$ with constant $L$ on $[t_0, t_0+T]$, and let $y$ solve the [initial value problem](c:initial-value-problem) $y' = f(t,y)$ with $\|y''\| \le M$. For the Euler steps $u_{n+1} = u_n + h f(t_n, u_n)$ with $u_0 = y(t_0)$, the error satisfies $\varepsilon_n \le \frac{Mh}{2L}(e^{L(t_n - t_0)} - 1)$ for $L > 0$, and $\varepsilon_n \le Mh(t_n - t_0)/2$ for $L = 0$.

hypotheses.text: The field $f$ satisfies $\|f(t,x) - f(t,y)\| \le L\|x - y\|$ for all $t$ in the interval.
The solution $y$ is $C^2$ with $\|y''\| \le M$ on the interval.
The initial value is exact: $u_0 = y(t_0)$.

conclusion: For every $n \le N$, the error $\varepsilon_n = \|y(t_n) - u_n\|$ obeys the stated bound. In particular, $\max_n \varepsilon_n \le C h$ with $C = (M/(2L))(e^{LT} - 1)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the inequality $1 + x \le e^x$, which is one step of the proof. It does not state the error bound.

proofs.name: One-step error and discrete Gronwall
proofs.slogan: Bound the local error by Taylor's formula, add the Lipschitz growth, and solve the recursion by induction.
proofs.scope: The whole statement with an exact initial value. An initial error $\varepsilon_0$ adds the term $\varepsilon_0 e^{L(t_n - t_0)}$. Rounding errors are not modeled.

roles.why: The Lipschitz bound turns the difference of the fields into the factor $hL\varepsilon_n$.
The bound on $y''$ limits the local error by $Mh^2/2$.
An exact start gives $\varepsilon_0 = 0$ for the induction.

steps.slogan: Bound the Taylor remainder $r = y(t_{n+1}) - y(t_n) - h y'(t_n)$.
steps.detail: We have $r = \int_0^h [y'(t_n + s) - y'(t_n)]\,ds$. The mean value inequality gives $\|y'(t_n+s) - y'(t_n)\| \le Ms$. So $\|r\| \le Mh^2/2$.

steps.slogan: Derive the one-step inequality $\varepsilon_{n+1} \le (1+hL)\varepsilon_n + Mh^2/2$.
steps.detail: Since $y' = f(t,y)$, we get $y(t_{n+1}) - u_{n+1} = (y(t_n) - u_n) + h[f(t_n, y(t_n)) - f(t_n, u_n)] + r$. Take norms, use the Lipschitz bound on the bracket, and use the remainder bound on $r$.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that $\varepsilon_n \le (Mh^2/2)\sum_{j<n} q^j$ with $q = 1 + hL$.
steps.detail: For $n = 0$ the claim holds because $\varepsilon_0 = 0$. If it holds for $n$, the one-step inequality gives $\varepsilon_{n+1} \le q(Mh^2/2)\sum_{j<n} q^j + Mh^2/2 = (Mh^2/2)\sum_{j \le n} q^j$.

steps.slogan: Sum the [geometric series](c:geometric-series) in the cases $L > 0$ and $L = 0$.
steps.detail: For $L > 0$, $\sum_{j<n} q^j = (q^n - 1)/(hL)$, so $\varepsilon_n \le \frac{Mh}{2L}(q^n - 1)$. For $L = 0$, $q = 1$ and the sum is $n$, so $\varepsilon_n \le nMh^2/2 = Mh(t_n - t_0)/2$.

steps.slogan: Replace $q^n$ by an [exponential function](c:exponential-function) bound.
steps.detail: The inequality $1 + x \le e^x$ gives $q \le e^{hL}$, so $q^n \le e^{L(t_n - t_0)}$. Insert this in the geometric bound. Then use $t_n - t_0 \le T$ to get the constant $C$.

concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: The Lipschitz bound controls how the error grows in one step.
concepts.c:initial-value-problem: The exact solution and the Euler iterates share the same initial value.
concepts.c:geometric-series: The recursion solves to a geometric sum.
concepts.c:exponential-function: The factor $(1+hL)^n$ is bounded by an exponential.

statement: Let $F(u,p)$ be $C^2$ and let $y$ be a $C^2$ solution of the [Euler-Lagrange equation](c:euler-lagrange-equation) $\frac{d}{dx}F_p(y,y') = F_u(y,y')$. Then $F(y,y') - y' F_p(y,y')$ is constant. For $F = u\sqrt{1+p^2}$ with $y > 0$, the constant is $c = y/\sqrt{1+y'^2}$. Where $y' \ne 0$, we get $y = c\cosh(x/c + \alpha)$, a [catenoid](c:minimal-surface) profile.

hypotheses.text: The Lagrangian $F$ does not depend on $x$.
The curve $y$ is $C^2$ and satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation on $[a,b]$.
For the catenoid, $y > 0$ on the interval, and $y' \ne 0$ for the last claim.

conclusion: The function $H = F(y,y') - y'F_p(y,y')$ is constant on $[a,b]$. For the catenoid Lagrangian, $y = c\cosh(x/c + \alpha)$ with $c > 0$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the product rule for derivatives, which is one step of the proof. It does not state the Beltrami identity.

proofs.name: Differentiate H and use the Euler-Lagrange equation
proofs.slogan: Differentiate $H$ along the curve, show that its derivative is zero, then solve the catenoid equation with hyperbolic functions.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The division by $y'$ in the catenoid part fails where $y' = 0$. The identity gives a first integral, not existence of a minimizer.

roles.why: Without explicit $x$ in $F$, the derivative of $F$ along the curve has no extra term.
The Euler-Lagrange equation makes the derivative of $H$ vanish.
Positivity gives $c > 0$ and fixes the sign of the coefficient $A$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate $F(y,y')$ and $y'F_p(y,y')$ along the curve.
steps.detail: The chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dx}F(y,y') = F_u y' + F_p y''$. The product rule gives $\frac{d}{dx}[y'F_p] = y''F_p + y'\frac{d}{dx}[F_p]$.

steps.slogan: Subtract and apply the Euler-Lagrange equation to get $H' = 0$.
steps.detail: We have $H' = F_u y' + F_p y'' - y''F_p - y'\frac{d}{dx}[F_p] = y'(F_u - \frac{d}{dx}F_p)$. The bracket is $0$ by the Euler-Lagrange equation. So $H$ is constant on the interval.

steps.slogan: Compute $H$ for $F = u\sqrt{1+p^2}$.
steps.detail: Here $F_p = up/\sqrt{1+p^2}$, so $F - pF_p = u/\sqrt{1+p^2}$. Hence $y/\sqrt{1+y'^2} = c$ for a constant $c$, and $c > 0$ because $y > 0$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the squared identity to get $y'' = y/c^2$.
steps.detail: Squaring gives $y^2 = c^2(1+y'^2)$. Differentiating gives $2yy' = 2c^2 y'y''$. Where $y' \ne 0$, divide by $2y'$ to get $y = c^2 y''$.

steps.slogan: Solve the linear equation and fix the constants with the [hyperbolic functions](c:hyperbolic-function).
steps.detail: The solutions are $y = A\cosh(x/c) + B\sinh(x/c)$. Inserting into $y^2 - c^2 y'^2 = c^2$ gives $A^2 - B^2 = c^2$. If $A < 0$, then $y < 0$, so $A > 0$. Put $\alpha = \operatorname{artanh}(B/A)$. Then $A = c\cosh\alpha$, $B = c\sinh\alpha$, and the addition formula gives $y = c\cosh(x/c + \alpha)$.

concepts.c:euler-lagrange-equation: The Euler-Lagrange equation makes the derivative of $H$ vanish.
concepts.c:minimal-surface: The catenoid is the minimal surface of revolution from this first integral.
concepts.c:hyperbolic-function: Solutions of $y'' = y/c^2$ are hyperbolic cosines and sines.

statement: Let $G$ be a finite simple [graph](c:graph) with [adjacency matrix](c:adjacency-matrix) $A$. Then $(A^k)_{uv}$ counts the walks of length $k$ from $u$ to $v$, and $\operatorname{tr}(A^k)$ counts the closed walks. So $\operatorname{tr}A^2 = 2|E|$ and $\operatorname{tr}A^3 = 6t$ for $t$ triangles. Also $\operatorname{tr}(A^k) = \sum_i \lambda_i^k$ for the [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue), and the diameter is at most $D$ if and only if $(I+A)^D > 0$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and undirected, with no loops and no multiple edges.
A walk of length $k$ is a vertex sequence $v_0, \dots, v_k$ with $v_{i-1}$ adjacent to $v_i$. Vertices may repeat.

conclusion: The entries of $A^k$ count walks, $\operatorname{tr}A^k$ counts closed walks with $\operatorname{tr}A^3 = 6t$ and $\operatorname{tr}A^k = \sum_i \lambda_i^k$, and the diameter test holds.

formal.difference: The declaration states the walk count for the entries of $A^k$, which is part (1). It does not state the trace, eigenvalue or diameter claims.

proofs.name: Induction on the walk length
proofs.slogan: Count walks by induction on the length, then read traces, eigenvalues and distances from the powers of $A$.
proofs.scope: The whole statement for a finite simple graph. Connectivity is part of the diameter test.

roles.why: No loops give a zero diagonal. Symmetry of $A$ gives the spectral theorem. Finiteness gives a finite trace.
Repeated vertices are allowed, so a walk extends by one step from any end vertex.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction on $k$ that $(A^k)_{uv}$ counts walks of length $k$ from $u$ to $v$.
steps.detail: For $k = 0$, $A^0 = I$ counts the walk of length $0$. A walk of length $k+1$ from $u$ to $v$ is a walk of length $k$ from $u$ to some $w$, followed by an edge $wv$. So the number is $\sum_w (A^k)_{uw} A_{wv} = (A^{k+1})_{uv}.

steps.slogan: Sum the diagonal to count closed walks, and read off the cases $k = 1, 2, 3$.
steps.detail: A closed walk of length $k$ from $u$ is a walk from $u$ to $u$, so the total is $\operatorname{tr}(A^k)$. For $k = 1$ it is a loop, so $\operatorname{tr}A = 0$. For $k = 2$ it is $u, w, u$, and the count is $\sum_u \deg u = 2|E|$. For $k = 3$ the three vertices are pairwise adjacent and distinct. Each triangle gives $6$ closed walks, so $\operatorname{tr}A^3 = 6t$.

steps.slogan: Diagonalize the symmetric matrix $A$ to get $\operatorname{tr}(A^k) = \sum_i \lambda_i^k$.
steps.detail: The matrix $A$ is real and symmetric. The spectral theorem gives an orthogonal $Q$ with $A = Q \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i) Q^T$. Then $A^k = Q \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i^k) Q^T$. The [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) is invariant under conjugation.

steps.slogan: Show that the distance is the least $k$ with $(A^k)_{uv} > 0$.
steps.detail: The distance from $u$ to $v$ is the length of a shortest walk. By the walk count, a walk of length $k$ exists exactly when $(A^k)_{uv} > 0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $(I+A)^D$ to test the diameter.
steps.detail: We have $(I+A)^D = \sum_{j=0}^D \binom{D}{j} A^j$, with nonnegative entries and positive coefficients. An entry is positive exactly when some $A^j$ with $j \le D$ is positive there. By the distance step this means that all pairs are at distance at most $D$. The case $u = v$ comes from $j = 0$.

steps.slogan: Collect the walk count, the trace formulas, the eigenvalue formula and the diameter test.
steps.detail: The walk step proves part (1). The closed walk step proves part (2). The spectral step proves part (3). The distance and diameter steps prove part (4).

concepts.c:graph: The theorem counts walks in a finite simple graph.
concepts.c:adjacency-matrix: The powers of this matrix encode the walks.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The eigenvalues turn the trace of a power into a power sum.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The trace sums the diagonal and counts closed walks.

statement:
Let $G$ be a finite simple [graph](c:graph) with $n$ vertices. Let $\alpha$ be the size of a largest [independent set](c:independent-set), $	au$ of a smallest [vertex cover](c:vertex-cover), $
u$ of a largest [matching](c:matching), and $ho$ of a smallest edge cover. Then $\alpha + 	au = n$ and $
u \le 	au \le 2
u$. If $G$ has no isolated vertex, then $ho + 
u = n$.

hypotheses.text: The graph $G$ is finite and simple.
For the edge cover identity, every vertex lies on at least one edge.

conclusion:
The identities $\alpha + 	au = n$ and $ho + 
u = n$ hold, and $
u \le 	au \le 2
u$ holds.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the complement of an independent set is a vertex cover and conversely. It does not state the inequalities or the edge cover identity.

proofs.name: Complements and a minimum edge cover forest
proofs.slogan: Use complements for the first identity, a maximal matching for the inequalities, and a minimum edge cover forest for the last identity.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The edge cover exists only when no vertex is isolated.

roles.why: Finiteness gives extremal sets, and simplicity gives well defined edges.
Without isolated vertices, every unmatched vertex has an edge to add.

steps.slogan: Show that complement is a bijection from independent sets to vertex covers, so $\alpha + \tau = n$.
steps.detail: If $I$ is independent, each edge has an end outside $I$, so $V \setminus I$ is a cover. If $C$ is a cover, no edge has both ends outside $C$, so $V \setminus C$ is independent. The map $I \mapsto V \setminus I$ sends size $k$ to size $n - k$. So $\tau = n - \alpha$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\nu \le \tau$ by charging each matching edge to a cover vertex.
steps.detail: Let $M$ be a matching and $C$ a cover. Each edge of $M$ has an end in $C$. The edges of $M$ share no ends, so these ends are distinct. Hence $|C| \ge |M|$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\tau \le 2\nu$ with the ends of a maximum matching.
steps.detail:
Let $M$ be a matching with $
u$ edges. If an edge had both ends outside the $2
u$ ends of $M$, we could add it to $M$. So the ends of $M$ form a vertex cover of size $2
u$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\rho \le n - \nu$ by extending a maximum matching.
steps.detail:
The $2
u$ ends of a maximum matching $M$ are covered by $M$. Each of the other $n - 2
u$ vertices lies on an edge. Choose one such edge for each. This gives an edge cover with at most $
u + (n - 2
u) = n - 
u$ edges.

steps.slogan: Show that $\rho \ge n - \nu$ by studying a minimum edge cover.
steps.detail: Let $F$ be a minimum edge cover. Each edge of $F$ has an end of degree $1$ in $F$, or $F$ minus that edge is a smaller cover. So $F$ has no cycle and is a forest with $c$ components, and $|F| = n - c$. One edge from each component gives a matching of size $c$, so $c \le \nu$ and $\rho \ge n - \nu$.

steps.slogan: Collect the identities and the inequalities.
steps.detail:
The steps prove $\alpha + 	au = n$, $
u \le 	au \le 2
u$, and $ho = n -

statement: Let $G$ act faithfully and [primitively](c:primitive-group) on a set $X$ with at least $2$ points. Suppose that each $x \in X$ has an abelian subgroup $T(x)$ with $T(gx) = gT(x)g^{-1}$, and that these subgroups generate $G$. Then every [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$ acting non trivially contains the [commutator subgroup](c:commutator-subgroup). If $G$ is perfect, $G$ is a [simple group](c:simple-group).

hypotheses.text: The action is faithful and primitive on $X$ with $|X| \ge 2$.
Each $T(x)$ is abelian, $T(gx) = gT(x)g^{-1}$, and the $T(x)$ generate $G$.

conclusion: Every normal subgroup $N$ that acts non trivially contains $[G,G]$. If $G = [G,G]$, then $G$ is simple.

formal.difference: The declaration states the simplicity of a perfect group with an Iwasawa structure. It is the second claim in a bundled form and does not state the first claim.

proofs.name: Orbits of a normal subgroup are blocks
proofs.slogan: Show that a normal subgroup is transitive or trivial, then show that it contains the commutator subgroup.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The groups $T(x)$ need not lie in the stabilizer of $x$.

roles.why: Primitivity makes the orbits of $N$ trivial or full, and faithfulness turns trivial orbits into $N = 1$.
The conjugation rule and generation give $G = N T(a)$, so $G/N$ is a quotient of an abelian group.

steps.slogan: Show that each orbit of a normal subgroup $N$ is a block.
steps.detail: For $g \in G$, $g(Nx) = (gNg^{-1})(gx) = N(gx)$. So $g(Nx)$ is an orbit of $N$. Two orbits of $N$ are equal or disjoint, so $Nx$ is a block.

steps.slogan: Show that $N$ is trivial or transitive.
steps.detail: By primitivity each $N$-orbit is a point or $X$. If one orbit is a point $x$, then for $y = gx$ and $n \in N$ we have $ny = g(g^{-1}ng)x = y$. So $N$ fixes every point, and $N = 1$ by faithfulness. Otherwise $N$ is [transitive](c:transitive-action) on $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that $G = N\,T(a)$ for a fixed point $a$ when $N$ is transitive.
steps.detail: Put $K = N T(a)$, a subgroup since $N$ is normal. For $x = na$, $T(x) = nT(a)n^{-1} \le K$. The $T(x)$ generate $G$, so $K = G$.

steps.slogan: Deduce that $G/N$ is abelian, so $[G,G] \le N$.
steps.detail: Every coset $gN$ equals $tN$ for some $t \in T(a)$. So $G/N$ is a quotient of the abelian group $T(a)$. A quotient $G/N$ is abelian if and only if $[G,G] \le N$.

steps.slogan: Show that a perfect group of this kind is simple.
steps.detail: Let $N$ be normal. If $N$ acts trivially, then $N = 1$ by faithfulness. Otherwise $N \ge [G,G] = G$. So $N = G$. Since $G$ is not trivial, $G$ is simple.

concepts.c:primitive-group: Primitivity forces each normal subgroup to be trivial or transitive.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: Normality makes the orbits blocks and makes $N T(a)$ a subgroup.
concepts.c:commutator-subgroup: The goal is to show that $N$ contains it.
concepts.c:simple-group: A perfect group with the property has no proper normal subgroup.
concepts.c:transitive-action: A non trivial normal subgroup acts transitively.

statement: Let $R$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $\preceq$ a [monomial order](c:monomial-order) on the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x_1, \dots, x_n]$. Let $b_1, \dots, b_s$ have unit leading coefficients. Then each $f$ has the form $f = \sum g_i b_i + r$ with $\deg(g_i b_i) \preceq \deg f$, and no monomial of $r$ is divisible by a leading monomial of any $b_i$.

hypotheses.text: The order $\preceq$ is total on $\mathbb{N}^n$, respects addition, and satisfies $0 \preceq a$ for all $a$.
Each $b_i$ is nonzero, and its leading coefficient is a unit of $R$.

conclusion: For every $f$ there are $g_1, \dots, g_s$ and $r$ with $f = \sum g_i b_i + r$, the degree bound, and a remainder free of divisible monomials.

formal.difference: The declaration states the same division with a remainder for a monomial order in mathlib. It is a related form and does not state the degree bound in these words.

proofs.name: Induction on the degree
proofs.slogan: Show that the order is a well order, then reduce the leading term of $f$ or move it to the remainder.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The result gives existence only, not uniqueness of $g_i$ and $r$.

roles.why: Compatibility with addition and $0 \preceq a$ make the order a well order and keep the cancelled terms small.
A unit leading coefficient lets us cancel the leading term of $f$ with no division.

steps.slogan: Show that the monomial order is a well order on exponent vectors.
steps.detail: Every sequence in $\mathbb{N}^n$ has indices $i < j$ with $a^i \le a^j$ in every coordinate, by repeated non-decreasing subsequences. Then $a^j = a^i + c$, and $0 \preceq c$ gives $a^i \preceq a^j$. So no infinite strictly decreasing sequence exists.

steps.slogan: Set up the induction on $\deg f$ with the trivial case $f = 0$.
steps.detail: Take $f \ne 0$ with $d = \deg f$ and leading coefficient $c$. Assume the claim for every polynomial of degree below $d$. The case $f = 0$ holds with all $g_i = 0$ and $r = 0$.

steps.slogan: If some $\deg b_i$ divides $x^d$, cancel the leading term and apply the hypothesis.
steps.detail: Put $u = c\,\ell^{-1} x^{d - \deg b_i}$ with $\ell = \operatorname{lc}(b_i)$. Then $f' = f - u b_i$ has no term $x^d$, so $f' = 0$ or $\deg f' \prec d$. Induction gives $f' = \sum g_j' b_j + r'$. Put $g_i = g_i' + u$, and keep the other $g_j$ and $r = r'$.

steps.slogan: If no $\deg b_i$ divides $x^d$, move the leading term to the remainder.
steps.detail: Write $f = c x^d + f_1$ with $f_1 = 0$ or $\deg f_1 \prec d$. Induction gives $f_1 = \sum g_j b_j + r_1$. Put $r = r_1 + c x^d$. The monomial $x^d$ is divisible by no $\deg b_i$, so $r$ has the required property.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the degree bound holds and that the process ends.
steps.detail: Both cases give $\deg(g_i b_i) \preceq \deg f$ for $g_i b_i \ne 0$. Each step lowers the degree of the working polynomial in a well order, so the algorithm ends.

concepts.c:monomial-order: The order decides which term is leading and gives the well order.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The statement is about division in a multivariate polynomial ring.

statement: Let $R \subseteq S$ be commutative rings with $S$ an [integral extension](c:integral-extension) of $R$. If $Q \subsetneq Q'$ are [prime ideals](c:prime-ideal) of $S$, then $Q \cap R \subsetneq Q' \cap R$. A prime $Q$ of $S$ is [maximal](c:maximal-ideal) if and only if $Q \cap R$ is maximal. So the [Krull dimension](c:krull-dimension) of $S$ is at most that of $R$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a subring of $S$ with the same identity.
Every element of $S$ is a root of a monic polynomial over $R$.

conclusion: Incomparability holds, $Q$ is maximal if and only if $Q \cap R$ is maximal, and $\dim S \le \dim R$.

formal.difference: The declaration states incomparability for an integral extension, which is part (a). It does not state the maximal ideal correspondence or the dimension bound.

proofs.name: Reduction to domains and a monic equation with nonzero constant term
proofs.slogan: Reduce to an extension of domains, find a monic equation with nonzero constant term, and read each claim from it.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. The dimension bound uses only part (a).

roles.why: Contraction $Q \cap R$ is a prime of $R$ and $R/(Q \cap R)$ embeds in $S/Q$.
Monic equations give the key lemma and the inverse of $a$ in the maximal case.

steps.slogan: Reduce the claims to an extension of [domains](c:integral-domain) $\bar R \subseteq \bar S$.
steps.detail: Let $p = Q \cap R$. The map $R/p \to S/Q$ is injective. The ring $S/Q$ is a domain, and it is integral over $R/p$, since a monic equation reduces mod $Q$ to a monic equation.

steps.slogan: Show that a nonzero $x \in \bar S$ satisfies a monic equation with nonzero constant term $a_0 \in x\bar S$.
steps.detail: Take a monic equation of least degree $n$. If $a_0 = 0$, then $x(x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1) = 0$. The domain property gives a monic equation of smaller degree, or $1 = 0$ when $n = 1$. Both are impossible. Also $a_0 = -x(x^{n-1} + \dots + a_1)$ lies in $x\bar S$.

steps.slogan: Prove incomparability by contradiction with the key lemma.
steps.detail: Let $Q \subsetneq Q'$ with $Q \cap R = Q' \cap R = p$. Pick $x \in Q' \setminus Q$. In $S/Q$ the image of $x$ is nonzero, and the lemma gives $a_0 \ne 0$ in $R/p$ with $a_0 \in \bar x \bar S \subseteq Q'/Q$. Then the lift of $a_0$ lies in $Q' \cap R = p$, so $a_0 = 0$. This is a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Prove that $Q$ is maximal if and only if $Q \cap R$ is maximal.
steps.detail: If $p = Q \cap R$ is maximal, then $\bar R$ is a field. For $x \ne 0$ in $\bar S$, $a_0 = -xy$ is a unit, so $x$ has an inverse and $Q$ is maximal. If $\bar S$ is a field, then for $a \ne 0$ in $\bar R$ the inverse $a^{-1}$ is integral over $\bar R$. Multiply its monic equation by $a^{m-1}$ to put $a^{-1}$ in $\bar R$. So $p$ is maximal.

steps.slogan: Contract a strict chain of primes of $S$ to a strict chain of primes of $R$.
steps.detail: Let $Q_0 \subsetneq \dots \subsetneq Q_n$ be primes of $S$. By incomparability the contractions $Q_i \cap R$ form a strict chain of primes of $R$ of length $n$. Taking the supremum gives $\dim S \le \dim R$.

steps.slogan: Collect the three claims.
steps.detail: The steps prove incomparability, the correspondence of maximal primes, and the dimension bound.

concepts.c:integral-extension: Integral elements give the monic equations used in every step.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: Contractions of primes of $S$ are primes of $R$.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: The correspondence of maximal ideals is part (b).
concepts.c:krull-dimension: Strict chains of primes bound the dimension.
concepts.c:integral-domain: The quotients by primes are domains, so the key lemma applies.

statement: Let $T_0 = 1$, $T_1 = x$ and $T_{k+1} = 2xT_k - T_{k-1}$. Then $T_n(\cos\theta) = \cos(n\theta)$, and $2^{1-n}T_n$ is a [monic polynomial](c:monic-polynomial) of degree $n$. A monic real polynomial $p$ of degree $n \ge 1$ has $\max_{[-1,1]}|p| \ge 2^{1-n}$, with equality if and only if $p = 2^{1-n}T_n$. This is the best [polynomial approximation](c:polynomial-approximation) of $x^n$ by lower degree.

hypotheses.text: The degree $n \ge 1$ is an integer.
The polynomial $p$ has real coefficients and leading coefficient $1$.
The norm is the supremum on the closed interval $[-1,1]$.

conclusion: The polynomial $T_n$ has degree $n$, leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, $n$ zeros and $n+1$ extrema of value $\pm 1$. The monic polynomial of least sup norm is $2^{1-n}T_n$, with norm $2^{1-n}$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the recurrence for Chebyshev polynomials. It does not state the minimax property.

proofs.name: Equioscillation and a root count
proofs.slogan: Show that a smaller monic competitor would make the difference with $2^{1-n}T_n$ have too many roots.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Equality in the norm forces $p = 2^{1-n}T_n$ because the root count is sharp.

roles.why: The degree $n$ gives $n+1$ extreme points and the root bound $n-1$ for the difference.
Monic polynomials of degree $n$ have a difference of degree below $n$.
The sup norm bounds $|p|$ at the extreme points and gives the sign pattern.

steps.slogan: Prove the cosine form, the degree, the leading coefficient and the bound $|T_n| \le 1$.
steps.detail: Induction on the recurrence gives degree $k$ and leading coefficient $2^{k-1}$ for $k \ge 1$. The identity $\cos((k+1)\theta) + \cos((k-1)\theta) = 2\cos\theta\cos(k\theta)$ gives $T_k(\cos\theta) = \cos(k\theta)$. So $|T_n| \le 1$ on $[-1,1]$.

steps.slogan: Find the $n$ zeros and the $n+1$ extreme points of $T_n$.
steps.detail: At $\theta = (2k-1)\pi/(2n)$, $\cos(n\theta) = 0$, and these $n$ points $\cos\theta$ are distinct, so they are all the roots. At $\theta = k\pi/n$, $T_n(x_k) = (-1)^k$ for the distinct points $x_k = \cos(k\pi/n)$, $0 \le k \le n$. The points $x_k$ with $0 < k < n$ are interior.

steps.slogan: Compare a monic $p$ with $q = 2^{1-n}T_n$ at the points $x_k$.
steps.detail: Let $\max|p| \le 2^{1-n}$ and $r = q - p$, of degree at most $n-1$. Suppose $r \ne 0$. With $\varepsilon_k = (-1)^k$, we have $\varepsilon_k r(x_k) \ge 0$ for all $k$. We show that this is impossible. A strict inequality $\max|p| < 2^{1-n}$ also gives $r \ne 0$ in the same way.

steps.slogan: Show that an interior zero of $r$ at an extreme point is a double zero.
steps.detail: If $0 < k < n$ and $r(x_k) = 0$, then $p(x_k) = q(x_k) = \varepsilon_k 2^{1-n}$. This value is the maximum or minimum of $p$ on $[-1,1]$, and $x_k$ is interior, so $p'(x_k) = 0$. The same holds for $q$. So $r'(x_k) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Count the roots of $r$ with multiplicity to get at least $n$.
steps.detail: Between consecutive indices with $r(x_k) \ne 0$, the sign change of $\varepsilon_k r(x_k)$ gives a root, or the skipped interior indices give double roots. Each gap $b - a$ holds at least $b - a$ roots. The two ends give at least $a_1$ and $n - a_s$ roots. The total is at least $n$. If no index has $r(x_k) \ne 0$, there are $n+1$ roots.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $r = 0$ and read the consequence for approximation by lower degree.
steps.detail: A nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ has at most $n-1$ roots with multiplicity. So $r = 0$ and $p = q$. For a polynomial $x^n - \tilde q$ with $\deg\tilde q < n$, the minimum norm $2^{1-n}$ is reached only by $\tilde q = x^n - 2^{1-n}T_n$.

concepts.c:monic-polynomial: The competitors and the difference with $2^{1-n}T_n$ rely on the monic condition.
concepts.c:polynomial-approximation: The theorem gives the best approximation of $x^n$ by lower degree.

statement: Let $f$ be $C^2$ on a closed interval $I$ with $f(x^*) = 0$, $|f'| \ge m > 0$ and $|f''| \le M$ on $I$. Put $c = M/(2m)$ and $N(x) = x - f(x)/f'(x)$. Then $|N(x) - x^*| \le c|x - x^*|^2$. If $c\rho < 1$ and $|x_0 - x^*| \le \rho$, [Newton's method](c:newton-s-method) gives $|x_k - x^*| \le c^{-1}(c|x_0 - x^*|)^{2^k}$ and $x_k \to x^*$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is $C^2$ on $I$ with $|f'| \ge m > 0$ and $|f''| \le M$, where $M > 0$.
The point $x^*$ in $I$ satisfies $f(x^*) = 0$.
The start satisfies $|x_0 - x^*| \le \rho$ with $[x^* - \rho, x^* + \rho] \subseteq I$ and $c\rho < 1$.

conclusion: The error satisfies the quadratic bound, the iterates stay in the ball and obey the explicit bound, they converge to $x^*$, and the ratio $(x_{k+1} - x^*)/(x_k - x^*)^2$ tends to $f''(x^*)/(2f'(x^*))$.

formal.difference: The declaration states a divisibility form of quadratic convergence of the Newton map for polynomials. It does not state the real interval bound.

proofs.name: Exact Taylor identity for the Newton step
proofs.slogan: Write the Newton error exactly by Taylor's formula, bound it, and iterate the bound.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. If $x_0 = x^*$, all iterates equal $x^*$ and the later claims are trivial.

roles.why: The lower bound on $|f'|$ allows the division, and the bounds give the constant $c$.
The condition $f(x^*) = 0$ is the left side of the Taylor expansion.
The condition $c\rho < 1$ keeps the iterates in the ball and makes the bound tend to $0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $f(x^*)$ around $x$ with the Lagrange remainder and solve for $x^* - N(x)$.
steps.detail: Taylor's formula ([Taylor series](c:taylor-series) to order 1) gives $\xi$ between $x$ and $x^*$ with $0 = f(x) + f'(x)(x^* - x) + \tfrac12 f''(\xi)(x^* - x)^2$. Divide by $f'(x)$. The left side is $x^* - N(x)$. So $x^* - N(x) = -f''(\xi)(x^* - x)^2/(2f'(x))$.

steps.slogan: Take absolute values to get the quadratic bound in part (1).
steps.detail: With $|f''| \le M$ and $|f'| \ge m$, the identity gives $|N(x) - x^*| \le \frac{M}{2m}|x - x^*|^2 = c|x - x^*|^2$.

steps.slogan: Show by induction that all iterates stay in the ball of radius $\rho$.
steps.detail: Assume $e_k = |x_k - x^*| \le \rho$. Then $c e_k \le c\rho < 1$, so $e_{k+1} \le c e_k e_k \le e_k \le \rho$. So $e_k$ does not increase, and every $x_k$ lies in the ball.

steps.slogan: Prove by induction that $c e_k \le (c e_0)^{2^k}$.
steps.detail: The case $k = 0$ is clear. If it holds for $k$, then $c e_{k+1} \le (c e_k)^2 \le (c e_0)^{2^{k+1}}$. Divide by $c > 0$ to get the bound in part (2).

steps.slogan: Show that the iterates converge and find the limit of the ratio.
steps.detail: Since $c e_0 < 1$, the power $(c e_0)^{2^k}$ tends to $0$, so $x_k \to x^*$. If $x_k \ne x^*$, the identity gives $(x_{k+1} - x^*)/(x_k - x^*)^2 = f''(\xi_k)/(2f'(x_k))$, with $\xi_k \to x^*$. Continuity of $f'$ and $f''$ gives the limit.

concepts.c:newton-s-method: The theorem bounds the error of this iteration near a simple root.
concepts.c:taylor-series: A Taylor expansion with Lagrange remainder gives the exact error identity.

statement: Let $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$ have the Lebesgue probability measure. The rotation $R_\alpha(x) = x + \alpha$ is [ergodic](c:ergodic) if and only if $\alpha$ is irrational. For an integer $m$ with $|m| \ge 2$, the doubling map $D_m(x) = mx \bmod 1$ is a [measure-preserving map](c:measure-preserving-map) and is ergodic. The proof uses the [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) of an invariant function.

hypotheses.text: The circle carries the Lebesgue probability measure.
In part (a), $\alpha$ is real. In part (b), $m$ is an integer with $|m| \ge 2$.

conclusion: The rotation $R_\alpha$ preserves the measure and is ergodic if and only if $\alpha$ is irrational. The map $D_m$ preserves the measure and is ergodic.

formal.difference: The declaration states that translation by a point of infinite order is ergodic on the additive circle. It is related to the irrational case and does not state the other cases.

proofs.name: Invariant functions have trivial Fourier coefficients
proofs.slogan: Show that an invariant set gives an invariant function, and that invariance kills all non zero Fourier coefficients.
proofs.scope: The whole statement. Part (a) splits into the irrational and the rational case.

roles.why: The measure is translation invariant, which gives measure preservation and a Fourier basis.
Irrational $\alpha$ gives $e^{2\pi i n\alpha} \ne 1$. A rational $\alpha$ gives an invariant set. A factor $|m| \ge 2$ makes the frequencies $m^j n$ distinct.

steps.slogan: Reduce ergodicity to showing that an invariant function is constant.
steps.detail: If $f \in L^2$ has $\hat f(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 0$, then Parseval gives $\|f - \hat f(0)\|^2 = 0$, so $f$ is constant almost everywhere. For an invariant set $A$, $f = 1_A$ satisfies $f \circ T = f$. If $f$ is constant, then $\lambda(A) \in \{0,1\}$.

steps.slogan: Check that $R_\alpha$ and $D_m$ preserve the measure.
steps.detail: Translation invariance of Lebesgue measure gives the claim for $R_\alpha$. For $D_m$ and an interval $I$, the preimage is a union of $|m|$ intervals of length $|I|/|m|$. Intervals form a generating $\pi$-system, so $\lambda \circ D_m^{-1} = \lambda$.

steps.slogan: For irrational $\alpha$, show that every invariant function has $\hat f(n) = 0$ for $n \ne 0$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of $f \circ R_\alpha$ at $n$ is $e^{2\pi i n\alpha}\hat f(n)$. Invariance gives $(e^{2\pi i n\alpha} - 1)\hat f(n) = 0$. For irrational $\alpha$ and $n \ne 0$, the factor is not zero, so $\hat f(n) = 0$.

steps.slogan: For rational $\alpha = p/q$, build a non trivial invariant set.
steps.detail: Let $A = \bigcup_{k=0}^{q-1} [k/q, k/q + 1/(2q))$. The map $R_\alpha$ permutes the $q$ intervals, so $R_\alpha^{-1}A = A$. Also $\lambda(A) = 1/2$. So $R_\alpha$ is not ergodic.

steps.slogan: For $D_m$, show that invariance forces $\hat f(n) = \hat f(m^j n)$, and that this tends to $0$.
steps.detail: The operator $Uf = f \circ D_m$ satisfies $U e_n = e_{mn}$, so the coefficient of $Uf$ at $mn$ is $\hat f(n)$. Invariance gives $\hat f(mn) = \hat f(n)$, hence $\hat f(n) = \hat f(m^j n)$ for all $j$. The integers $m^j n$ are distinct for $n \ne 0$. Bessel's inequality gives $\hat f(m^j n) \to 0$, so $\hat f(n) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases to conclude parts (a) and (b).
steps.detail: In the irrational case and for $D_m$, the invariant function is constant, so the map is ergodic by the reduction. The rational case is not ergodic, so part (a) holds.

concepts.c:ergodic: The theorem decides when every invariant set is null or of full measure.
concepts.c:measure-preserving-map: Invariance of the measure makes the composition operator an isometry.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: The coefficients of an invariant function show that it is constant.
